candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (trace a handover) and the trainee viewpoint led to following one number, the as-needed opioid dose, from the day team that raised the regular dose to the night trainee who inherits the chart; 'residue' and 'adjusting' suggested the leftover dose that was never adjusted.
candidates.working_title: When the regular opioid dose goes up, recalculate the as-needed dose
candidates.core_insight: When the regular 24-hour opioid dose is increased, for example in a syringe pump, the as-needed (rescue) dose on the chart usually needs recalculating at the same time, or the night team inherits a dose too small to help.
candidates.angle: Opioid titration in the last days of life usually happens on the day shift, while the as-needed dose written earlier still reflects the old 24-hour total. Following that one number across the handover shows where night-time symptom control fails: the trainee called at 3am gives the dose on the chart, it does little, and the next call follows. UK palliative care guidance links the as-needed dose to a fraction of the 24-hour dose, so the fix is to rewrite both in the same act and name both at handover.
candidates.position: Whenever the regular opioid dose changes, the prescriber should recalculate and rewrite the as-needed dose in the same act, and the handover should state both doses.
claims_needing_evidence: UK palliative care guidance sets the as-needed (breakthrough) opioid dose as a fraction of the total 24-hour regular dose, commonly one sixth, with some sources giving one tenth to one sixth (source: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines; EAPC opioid recommendations; Palliative Care Formulary).
When the 24-hour regular dose is changed, guidance advises recalculating the as-needed dose (source: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines, choosing and changing opioids; syringe pump guidance).
Guidance advises reviewing the number of as-needed doses used in 24 hours when adjusting the regular dose (source: NICE NG31 or NICE CG140; Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines).

An illustrative worked example (e.g. 30 mg subcutaneous morphine over 24 hours giving a 5 mg as-needed dose at one sixth) is arithmetically consistent with the guidance fraction (check against the guideline before use; label as illustrative).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (an outcome patients value that the routine measure misses) and the trial-designer viewpoint pointed to symptom scores as the usual recorded outcome and to mental awareness as a neglected one; 'permission' suggested asking the person how they weigh the two.
candidates.working_title: How alert do you want to be?
candidates.core_insight: Many seriously ill people rate staying mentally aware as important, so the balance between symptom relief and drowsiness near the end of life should be set by asking the person, and the answer recorded for when they can no longer say.
candidates.angle: Services and trials usually record pain and symptom scores. In Steinhauser's US national survey, being mentally aware was one of the items seriously ill patients rated as important more often than doctors did. A drowsy but pain-free person may be a success on the chart and a loss to the person. Asking early, 'How alert do you want to be?', lets dose decisions reflect their priorities.
candidates.position: Before and during opioid or sedative titration near the end of life, clinicians should ask how the person weighs alertness against symptom relief, record the answer and review it.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US national survey of seriously ill patients, bereaved relatives, doctors and other care providers, 'being mentally aware' received strong importance ratings from patients but less from doctors (Steinhauser 2000, JAMA; PubMed abstract seen).
In the same survey, freedom from pain ranked most important of 9 major attributes, and pain and symptom management was rated important by all groups (Steinhauser 2000; abstract seen).
Drowsiness is a common effect when strong opioids are started or the dose is increased and often settles within days (NICE CG140 patient information recommendations; verify wording).
Symptom-relief doses can be adjusted to balance comfort and alertness, guided by the person's wishes (NICE NG31 individualised care; verify).

candidates.gain: One question that makes dose decisions follow the person's own priorities.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (ask what would change the decision), the spouse viewpoint and 'the first hour' led to the decision families face in the first hour after an expected death at home, whether to call 999, which turns on whether the death was expected; 'delay' suggested telling families there is no need to hurry.
candidates.working_title: Who to phone when an expected death happens at home
candidates.core_insight: When someone dies at home and the death was expected, the family does not need to call an ambulance or hurry; they can phone the GP practice, district nursing team or out-of-hours service to have the death verified, and take time with the person first.
candidates.angle: Families caring for a dying person at home are told a lot about symptoms and little about the hour after the death. Asking in advance, 'If he dies at night, who do we phone?', changes that hour for a husband or wife: they know an expected death is not an emergency, they have the number, and they know there is time to sit with the person before anyone arrives.
candidates.position: Every family caring for someone expected to die at home should be told, before the death, whom to phone afterwards, day and night, and that there is no need to rush.
claims_needing_evidence: When a death at home is expected, 999 is not needed; families contact the GP practice, district nurses or the out-of-hours service (NHS 111 in England and Wales; NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland) (source: NHS inform 'What to do when someone dies'; nhs.uk equivalent; Marie Curie information).

In many UK services, registered nurses as well as doctors can verify an expected death (source: Hospice UK guidance on registered nurse verification of expected adult death; Scottish guidance on verification of expected death).
Families can spend time with the person before verification and before contacting a funeral director (source: Hospice UK 'Care after death' guidance).
If a death is sudden or unexpected, families should call 999 (source: NHS guidance).
If an ambulance is called, crews may start CPR unless a DNACPR or ReSPECT form is available (source: JRCALC guidance or Resuscitation Council UK; verify before including).

candidates.stimulus_use: Reversing the default assumption, from the older person's viewpoint, targeted the belief that almost everyone wants to die at home; 'drift' suggested that preferences change as illness advances.
candidates.working_title: Do most people want to die at home?
candidates.core_insight: The common statement that most people want to die at home rests on studies that often leave out people who were never asked or had no preference, so each person's own preference, which may be a hospice, hospital or care home, needs asking and may change.
candidates.angle: Policy and audit often treat home death as the aim and count it as success. Hoare and colleagues' review of UK studies found preferences were often missing, and that once missing data were included it was not known what proportion preferred home; where people were asked also influenced the answer. In a US survey, dying at home ranked lowest of nine major attributes. For an older person the preference may be about who is there, pain relief, or not exhausting a husband or wife, more than the building.
candidates.position: Services should ask each person where they would prefer to be cared for and to die, record the reasons, review the answer, and not count a well-planned death in a hospital, hospice or care home as a failure.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of UK studies (2000 to 2015, 61 studies) found missing preferences for place of death were common; when missing data were included, the proportion preferring home was unknown (Hoare 2015, PLoS One; abstract seen).
The same review found that where people wished to die was related to where they were asked (Hoare 2015; abstract seen).
In a US national survey, dying at home ranked least important of 9 major end-of-life attributes, with wide variation (Steinhauser 2000; abstract seen).
Some people's preferred place of death changes as illness progresses (Gomes 2013 BMC Palliative Care review; verify).

Home death or 'preferred place of death achieved' is used as an indicator of end-of-life care quality in UK reporting (OHID palliative and end of life care profiles; Public Health Scotland indicators; verify).

candidates.stimulus_use: Reversing the default assumption, provoked by 'noise' and 'the last week of life', led to the rattling breath of dying people and two defaults: families' belief that it means choking, and staff's assumption that every relative is distressed by it.
candidates.working_title: The noisy breathing near death
candidates.core_insight: Noisy, rattling breathing in the last hours or days happens when a dying person can no longer clear saliva and secretions from the throat; the person is usually deeply unconscious, and a change of position, a clear explanation and sometimes a medicine can help those listening.
candidates.angle: Relatives interviewed by Wee and colleagues were distressed when they thought the person was drowning or choking; others were not distressed, and some took the sound as a sign that death was near. So an explanation is itself a treatment for the listeners. Turning the person onto their side can reduce the sound; medicines reduce new secretions rather than clearing what is already there.
candidates.position: Staff should explain the sound to families as soon as it starts, ask how it is affecting them, and offer repositioning before or alongside medicines.
claims_needing_evidence: The sound comes from secretions in the throat and upper airways that the dying person can no longer cough or swallow (NICE NG31; Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines).
People with this sound are usually deeply unconscious, and it is thought unlikely to distress them (NICE NG31 wording to verify; this is inference, not measured, and must be phrased as such).
In cancer patients in acute palliative care units, death rattle occurred mostly in the last 3 days of life (Hui 2014, Oncologist; abstract seen).

In interviews, some bereaved relatives were distressed by the sound, particularly when they thought the person was choking or drowning, while others were not (Wee 2006 I and II, Palliative Medicine; abstracts seen: 5 of 12 and 10 of 25 relatives who heard it were distressed).
Repositioning can reduce the sound (NICE NG31 or Scottish guidelines; verify).
In a Dutch hospice RCT, prophylactic subcutaneous hyoscine butylbromide reduced death rattle from 27% to 13% (van Esch 2021, JAMA; abstract seen).

candidates.working_title: Is hearing the last sense to go?
candidates.core_insight: A small EEG study found that the brains of some unresponsive dying hospice patients still responded to sounds in a way similar to healthy young people, which supports talking to a dying person who is unable to respond, though it does not show that they understand the words.
candidates.angle: The saying is repeated at many bedsides, often by staff who do not know its basis. Blundon, Gallagher and Ward tested it with brain recordings in Vancouver hospices. The finding fits the advice to keep talking and to explain before touching; its limits are a small sample and a test of responses to tones, not comprehension.
candidates.position: Speak to an unresponsive dying person as if they may hear: say who is there, what you are doing and what you want to say.
claims_needing_evidence: Blundon et al. recorded EEG responses to changes in tones and tone patterns in hospice patients while responsive and again when unresponsive near death, and in young healthy controls (Sci Rep 2020; abstract seen).
Most unresponsive patients showed mismatch negativity responses to tone changes, and some showed P3a or P3b responses (abstract seen).
The number of unresponsive patients studied was small [N to verify from full text, PMC7316981].
The study measured brain responses to sounds; it did not test understanding of speech or conscious awareness (check the paper's discussion).
Guidance for families and staff encourages talking to a dying person who appears unresponsive (source: NICE NG31 or NHS/Marie Curie information; verify).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (compare what is recorded with what is experienced) and the physiotherapist viewpoint contrasted a record reading 'palliative' with a person's day organised around getting to the toilet; 'trade-offs' suggested steering between abandonment and burdensome therapy.
candidates.working_title: Palliative, and still getting to the toilet
candidates.core_insight: People with advanced illness often want to keep the ability to stand, move and reach the toilet, and physiotherapy and occupational therapy aimed at those goals remain part of good palliative care.
candidates.angle: A record that says 'palliative' can be read as a reason to stop therapy, while the person's own day may turn on whether they can reach the toilet, sit out for a visitor or wash at the sink. Rehabilitative palliative care keeps goals small and chosen by the person, and uses equipment, positioning and ways of saving energy.
candidates.position: A palliative care label should prompt a review of therapy goals with the person, not the end of therapy.
claims_needing_evidence: Hospice UK describes rehabilitative palliative care as integrating rehabilitation into palliative care to help people live as fully and independently as possible until they die (Tiberini and Richardson 2015, Hospice UK).

Systematic reviews report that rehabilitation for people with advanced cancer can maintain or improve physical function and quality of life (e.g. Salakari 2015, Acta Oncologica; verify; mostly cancer populations).
Independence in toileting and mobility is a priority for many people with advanced illness (source: qualitative studies; lead to find; drop if unsupported).
Therapy input is reduced once people are labelled palliative (source needed; if no study supports it, remove this claim and keep the positive framing).

candidates.working_title: Family members giving the injections: the trade-off
candidates.core_insight: In a UK feasibility trial, trained family carers gave as-needed injections for symptoms at home far faster than a nurse could arrive, but the approach shifts responsibility onto families and should be a free, supported choice, never a way to cover gaps in nursing.
candidates.angle: CARiAD found a median of 5 minutes to give the medicine when a trained carer did it, against 105 minutes in usual care, and carers felt confident. It also found professionals less ready than carers, and district nurses overstretched. The trade-off is speed and control against the weight of giving drugs to someone you love in their last days.
candidates.position: Carer-given injections can be offered to willing, trained carers with 24-hour professional back-up, but should never be expected of families or used to replace a timely nursing response.
claims_needing_evidence: CARiAD was a UK feasibility RCT of lay carer administration of as-needed subcutaneous medicine for breakthrough symptoms in people dying at home (Poolman 2020 HTA; Poolman 2025 BMJ Open; abstracts seen).
Median time to medication administration was 5 minutes in the intervention group and 105 minutes in usual care (BMJ Open 2025 abstract).
Carers were uniformly enthusiastic; health professionals were less ready to consider it; district nurses were overstretched (abstracts).
40 dyads were recruited, retention was unbalanced, and the success of a definitive trial was judged uncertain (abstracts).
Lay carer administration is established practice in some other countries, such as Australia (HTA abstract background; verify).

candidates.working_title: Ask the family how the last days went
candidates.core_insight: How someone dies is linked with how their relatives fare afterwards, so care of dying people should also be judged by asking bereaved relatives, not only by records that stop at the death.
candidates.angle: Routine end-of-life measures end at the death: place of death, forms completed, symptoms charted. In a US cohort of people with advanced cancer, more aggressive care in the final week was linked with a higher risk of major depression in bereaved caregivers; in an Australian trial in people aged 80 and over, relatives of those who died had less stress, anxiety and depression after facilitated advance care planning. National surveys of bereaved relatives exist but are not used everywhere.
candidates.position: Services should routinely ask bereaved relatives about care in the last days and use the answers to improve care.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US prospective cohort of 332 patients with advanced cancer and their caregivers, more aggressive medical care near death was associated with higher risk of major depressive disorder in bereaved caregivers (adjusted OR 3.37; observational) (Wright 2008, JAMA; abstract seen).

In an RCT of facilitated advance care planning in medical inpatients aged 80 and over, family members of those who died had less stress, anxiety and depression (Detering 2010, BMJ; abstract seen; small numbers).

candidates.position: Families should be told what each medicine in the box is for, who can give it, and that it may never be needed.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same operation (recorded versus experienced) applied to the repositioning chart: the chart records turns on schedule, the dying person experiences each turn.
candidates.working_title: Turning in the last days: by comfort, not by the clock
candidates.core_insight: In the last days of life, how often a person is repositioned should be agreed with them or their family and guided by comfort, with pain relief before turns that hurt, rather than set by a fixed schedule kept for the chart.
candidates.angle: The chart shows ticks every two hours; the person may experience each turn as pain. International pressure injury guidance has specific recommendations for palliative care that allow repositioning to follow the person's wishes, comfort and tolerance. Some skin damage at the end of life may occur despite good care, which is a reason for honest explanation, not for abandoning pressure care.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (find the first question worth asking), the GP viewpoint and 'the moment of discharge' led to the question a GP team can ask when a discharge letter arrives after an unplanned admission.
candidates.working_title: The discharge letter as a prompt
candidates.core_insight: An unplanned hospital admission in an older person with advancing illness is a recognised indicator of deteriorating health, and the GP team reading the discharge letter can use it to ask whether a conversation and plan about future care are needed.
candidates.angle: In a Scottish study of six practices, only about 1 in 5 people who died of non-cancer conditions had any palliative care documented before death, against about two thirds of people with cancer. SPICT, developed in Edinburgh, uses general indicators such as unplanned admissions to identify people who may benefit from planning, without predicting a date of death. The letter arriving after discharge is when the GP team first sees the signal.
candidates.position: GP teams should treat an unplanned admission of an older person with advancing frailty, dementia or organ failure as a prompt to review whether a future care conversation and plan are needed.
claims_needing_evidence: In six Scottish general practices, 29% of people who died had been on the palliative care register; about two thirds of people with cancer were on it, and around 20% of those with non-malignant conditions had any palliative care documented (Harrison 2012, BJGP; abstract seen; small study, older data).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (count something nobody counts), the daughter's viewpoint and 'the last week of life' led to counting the moves between settings near death, which place-of-death figures do not show.
candidates.working_title: Count the moves in the last days
candidates.core_insight: Moves between care home, emergency department and wards near death are common and can signal missed planning; in a US national study, nearly 1 in 5 nursing home residents with advanced cognitive and physical impairment had at least one burdensome transition near the end of life.
candidates.angle: A daughter can count the beds her mother passed through in her last week; routine UK statistics report where people die. Gozalo and colleagues defined burdensome transitions (a move in the last 3 days, several hospitalisations in the last 90 days, or not returning to the same home) and found wide regional variation and links with other markers of poor end-of-life care.
candidates.position: Services should count transfers in the last days of life as a measure of end-of-life care, alongside place of death.
claims_needing_evidence: Among 474,829 US nursing home decedents with advanced cognitive and functional impairment (2000 to 2007), 19.0% had at least one burdensome transition (Gozalo 2011, NEJM; abstract seen).

Rates varied by state from 2.1% to 37.5%, and were higher among Black and Hispanic residents and those without an advance directive (abstract seen).
Regions with more burdensome transitions had more feeding tubes, ICU use in the last month, stage IV pressure ulcers and late hospice enrolment (abstract seen).
UK routine indicators report place of death and hospital use in the last months of life but not transfers in the last 3 days (verify with OHID and Public Health Scotland indicators).

candidates.working_title: The last year of life is on every ward
candidates.core_insight: On a single census day in 25 Scottish hospitals, 28.8% of inpatients died within 12 months, and 45.6% of those aged 85 and over, so recognising possible last year of life and planning future care belong on ordinary wards.
candidates.angle: Palliative care is often pictured as a specialist service for a few identified patients. A count of every inpatient on one day shows how many hospital beds are occupied by people in their last year of life, most of whom will not have been identified as such.
candidates.position: Every hospital ward caring for older people should have staff able to recognise possible last year of life and start conversations about future care.

candidates.working_title: The surprise question is a prompt, not a prediction
candidates.core_insight: The question 'Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?' picks up only about two thirds of people who go on to die, and most people it flags are still alive a year later, so it works as a prompt to start planning, not as a forecast.
candidates.angle: The surprise question is built into UK identification guidance. Downar's meta-analysis found pooled sensitivity of 67% and positive predictive value of 37%, with worse performance in non-cancer illness. Using it to label someone 'end of life' or to limit treatment misreads it; using it to open a conversation about future care fits what it can do.
candidates.position: Use the surprise question to trigger conversations and care planning, never to predict a date or to restrict treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: Meta-analysis of 16 studies (17 cohorts, 11,621 patients) for death at 6 to 18 months: pooled sensitivity 67.0%, specificity 80.2%, positive predictive value 37.1%, negative predictive value 93.1% (Downar 2017, CMAJ; abstract seen).
Discrimination was worse in non-cancer illness than in cancer (abstract seen).
Most included studies had moderate to high risk of bias (abstract seen).
The surprise question is used in the Gold Standards Framework Proactive Identification Guidance (verify current edition).

candidates.working_title: Survival estimates run optimistic, most of all for patients you know well
candidates.core_insight: In a Chicago study of hospice referrals, doctors' survival predictions were accurate only 1 time in 5 and were usually too optimistic, and the longer the doctor had known the patient, the less accurate the prediction.
candidates.angle: The doctor who knows a patient best feels best placed to estimate how long they have; this study found the opposite. Practical corrections: give a range, say what signs would shorten it, and ask a colleague's view when you know the patient well.
candidates.position: Clinicians should give survival estimates as ranges, with the signs that would change them, and seek a second view when they know the patient well.
claims_needing_evidence: 343 doctors gave survival estimates for 468 terminally ill patients at hospice referral; median survival was 24 days (Christakis 2000, BMJ; abstract seen).
20% of predictions were accurate (within 33% of actual survival), 63% overoptimistic and 17% overpessimistic; overall overestimate by a factor of 5.3 (abstract seen).
Accuracy fell as the duration of the doctor-patient relationship increased and time since last contact decreased (abstract seen).
A later systematic review found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care often inaccurate (White 2016, PLoS One; verify).
Limits: US outpatient hospice programmes, late 1990s, mostly cancer (check paper).

candidates.working_title: Morphine and the fear that it means the end
candidates.core_insight: Being offered morphine or another strong opioid is a decision about pain or breathlessness; NICE tells doctors to ask about common fears, including the fear that it means the final stage of life, and to prescribe a laxative from the start.
candidates.angle: The belief that morphine signals the end keeps some people in pain. Naming the fear, and the guidance that tells doctors to ask about it, gives older people and families permission to raise it. A practical question about constipation shows what good prescribing includes.
candidates.position: People offered strong opioids should be asked about their fears, and every such prescription should come with a plan to prevent constipation.

candidates.working_title: Mouth care in the last days
candidates.core_insight: In the last days of life a dry mouth is common and uncomfortable; frequent mouth and lip care relieves it, families who wish to can help, and a drip does not reliably relieve thirst or other symptoms.
candidates.angle: Families often worry about thirst and ask for a drip. The comfort measure that acts directly on a dry mouth is mouth care, and it is something a relative can do. candidates.working_title: Breathlessness: a fan to the face, and oxygen for low oxygen levels
candidates.core_insight: For breathlessness in advanced illness, a hand-held fan blowing air across the face reduced breathlessness in a crossover trial, while oxygen gave no more relief than room air in people whose oxygen levels were not low.
candidates.angle: Oxygen is often given as a comfort measure; its tubing, noise, dry nose and limits on movement are real costs. Trials suggest air moving across the face helps, and that oxygen adds little without low oxygen levels. In a small study of patients near death, oxygen, air and no flow made no difference to respiratory distress for most.
candidates.position: Offer a fan, positioning and explanation first; use oxygen for low oxygen levels or as an individual trial, and stop it if it does not help.
claims_needing_evidence: Randomised crossover trial in 50 patients with advanced disease: a hand-held fan directed at the face reduced breathlessness compared with the fan directed at the legs (Galbraith 2010, J Pain Symptom Manage; abstract seen).

In a double-blind repeated-measures study of 32 patients near death, alternating oxygen, medical air and no flow produced no differences in respiratory distress; 91% tolerated the protocol (Campbell 2013, J Pain Symptom Manage; abstract seen).
Oxygen can cause nasal irritation and adds cost (Campbell 2013 abstract).

candidates.working_title: Parkinson's medicines when swallowing stops

candidates.working_title: Diabetes in the last days: fewer tests, and insulin still in type 1

candidates.working_title: Ask what the later stages of dementia usually bring
candidates.core_insight: Eating problems, fevers and chest infections are common in advanced dementia, and in a US study, residents whose families understood this and the likely prognosis were much less likely to have burdensome interventions, such as hospital transfer or tube feeding, in their last three months.
candidates.angle: Dementia is often not recognised as an illness people die from. Families who have been told what usually happens can decide in advance about hospital, antibiotics and feeding, instead of meeting each decision for the first time in a crisis.
candidates.position: Families of people with advanced dementia should be told clearly what the later stages usually bring, and invited to plan.

candidates.working_title: Antibiotics for chest infection in advanced dementia: survival and comfort
candidates.core_insight: In a US study of nursing home residents with advanced dementia, antibiotic treatment of suspected pneumonia was linked with longer survival but not with better comfort, and oral antibiotics were linked with survival similar to injections, drips or hospital admission.

candidates.working_title: CPR on television and in real hospitals
candidates.core_insight: On popular TV medical dramas most people given CPR survive, while in UK hospitals fewer than 1 in 5 adults given CPR survive to leave hospital, so expectations formed by television can mislead decisions.
candidates.angle: Studies in 1996 and 2015 found TV survival after CPR far above real rates. Knowing the real figure, and that it varies with the cause of the arrest and the person's health, helps people take part in CPR decisions on realistic terms.
candidates.position: CPR conversations should give people realistic figures for their situation, and people can ask for them.
claims_needing_evidence: In 91 episodes of Grey's Anatomy and House (2010 to 2011), CPR was shown 46 times, with a survival rate of 69.6% (Portanova 2015, Resuscitation; abstract seen).

Survival is lower in frailer older people (Ibitoye 2021, Age and Ageing: small single-centre study in which no frail patients survived to discharge; abstract seen; treat as limited evidence).

candidates.working_title: Poorer neighbourhoods, more hospital deaths
candidates.core_insight: In high-income countries, people from more deprived areas are more likely to die in hospital rather than at home, more likely to receive hospital care in the last 3 months of life, and less likely to receive specialist palliative care.

candidates.working_title: Care homes are becoming the most common place to die
candidates.core_insight: If trends from 2004 to 2014 continue, deaths in care homes in England and Wales will more than double by 2040, making the care home the most common place of death, so end-of-life care in care homes is central to how many older people will die.
candidates.angle: Planning for end-of-life care is still often pictured around hospitals and hospices. Bone and colleagues' projection shows the care home as the growing setting, and care workers already do much of this work.
candidates.position: End-of-life care in care homes should be planned and supported as a main setting of dying, with training, time, and medical and specialist support for staff.
claims_needing_evidence: Between 2004 and 2014 in England and Wales, the proportion of deaths in care homes rose from 16.7% to 21.2% and at home from 18.3% to 22.9%, while hospital deaths fell from 57.9% to 48.1% (Bone 2018, Palliative Medicine; abstract seen).
If trends continue, care home deaths increase by 108.1% by 2040, making care homes the most common place of death (abstract seen).
Annual deaths projected to rise from 501,424 in 2014 to 635,814 in 2040, with 53.6% aged 85 and over (abstract seen).
The projection assumes continued trends and predates the COVID-19 pandemic (limitation).

candidates.working_title: Slow decline, and no clear moment
candidates.core_insight: People with frailty or dementia usually decline slowly over years from an already low level of function, so there may be no clear moment when anyone says they are dying, and conversations about the future are best started early.
candidates.angle: Published illness trajectories differ: cancer often has a period of stable function and then a steep fall; organ failure has dips and partial recoveries; frailty and dementia show low function and slow decline. Families of people with frailty often wait for a signal that never comes.
candidates.position: For people with advancing frailty or dementia, families and clinicians should start talking about future care while the person can still take part, without waiting for a turning point.
claims_needing_evidence: Lunney et al. (JAMA 2003) described patterns of functional decline in the last year of life among older US decedents: sudden death, cancer, organ failure and frailty (verify).
In the frailty pattern, function was low throughout the last year and declined progressively (verify).
Murray et al. (BMJ 2005) described three trajectories (cancer; organ failure; frailty and dementia) and their implications for palliative care (verify).
Tools predicting death perform worse in non-cancer illness (Downar 2017; abstract seen) (supporting context).

candidates.working_title: Palliative care can start alongside treatment
candidates.core_insight: Palliative care can start early in a serious illness, alongside treatment aimed at the illness, and in a well-known trial of early palliative care in advanced lung cancer, people had better quality of life and mood.
candidates.angle: Some people turn down palliative care because they think it means stopping treatment or dying soon. The World Health Organization describes it as applicable early, together with treatments intended to prolong life. The Temel trial was in younger people with lung cancer, so the ask for older people is help with symptoms, support and planning, not a promise of longer life.
candidates.position: People with serious illness can ask for palliative care support without giving up other treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: The WHO definition describes palliative care as applicable early in the course of illness, in conjunction with other therapies intended to prolong life (WHO 2002 definition; verify current wording).

In an RCT of 151 patients with newly diagnosed metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, early palliative care improved quality of life and mood, and fewer received aggressive end-of-life care (Temel 2010, NEJM; verify from abstract; survival difference was a secondary finding and should not lead).
Patients and carers often associate palliative care with death and loss of hope (Zimmermann 2016, CMAJ; verify).
The trial population differs from older people with frailty or non-cancer illness (limitation).
